---
title: "Herb care on an east-facing balcony"
---

Notes for culinary herbs on a **ground-floor, east-facing balcony in
Marseille** (Provençal south): strong morning sun, shade from midday
onwards, hot dry summers, mild winters, and occasional Mistral.

The morning sun is enough for Mediterranean herbs without the
scorching west-facing afternoon that burns basil and parsley in July
and August. Keep thyme in a **separate, drier pot**; grow basil, curly
parsley, chives, and dill in richer, moister compost.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-herb-pots
%%| fig-cap: "Suggested pot grouping for an east-facing Marseille balcony."
flowchart TD
  A[East balcony — morning sun] --> B[Moist pot]
  A --> C[Dry pot — thyme alone]
  A --> D[Tall pot — dill]
  B --> B1[Basil]
  B --> B2[Curly parsley]
  B --> B3[Chives]
```

## Site and watering {#sec-herb-site}

- **Orientation:** east — water in the evening in midsummer, or in the
  morning after the first hour of sun. Avoid wetting leaves in full
  sun.
- **Wind:** ground floor is calmer than upper storeys, but still
  shelter dill and basil from a strong Mistral with the wall or a
  light screen.
- **Drainage:** every pot needs holes and a saucer; empty standing
  water after watering so roots do not sit in a puddle.
- **Summer rhythm:** basil and parsley almost daily in a heatwave;
  chives every two days; thyme twice a week at most.

## Basil {#sec-basil}

*(basilic)*

- **Light / heat:** morning sun; afternoon shade in Marseille is an
  advantage. Bring the pot in if nights drop below about 10 °C.
- **Water:** keep the compost evenly moist, never waterlogged. Wilt in
  the afternoon is a cue to water that evening.
- **Humidity:** mist leaves in very dry Mistral weather; good air
  around the plant still matters (do not crowd).
- **Support:** none. See **Trimming** below.
- **Companions:** curly parsley and chives in the same wide pot.
  Keep thyme out of this mix.

### Trimming basil for harvest {#sec-basil-trim}

Follow the node-and-pair method from
[Les Sourciers — how to prune basil](https://lessourciers.com/fr/blog/2021/05/19/taille-basilic/).
Leaves sit in **pairs** on the stem; at each node, small axillary
buds can become new stems if you give them light.

1. Wait until the main stem has at least two well-formed leaf pairs
   with visible side buds.
2. Cut **just above a pair of buds**, leaving almost no stub (a long
   stub tends to rot).
3. Prefer the **second** pair from the base for the first cut, so the
   lower buds can thicken.
4. Each cut yields two new stems; repeat the same cut on those stems
   as they lengthen. That is how a single spike becomes a bush.
5. Use the leafy tip you removed. Do not strip single leaves from
   the lower stem — that is what produces a “bald stick”.

Flowering does **not** reverse if you keep cutting: the plant has
already switched. Stagger a second sowing for a continuous leaf crop.
Flowering tops are still edible (oil, drying); the leaves remain
edible but thinner.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-basil-trim
%%| fig-cap: "Basil: cut above a leaf-pair node so two side shoots take over."
flowchart TD
  A[Main stem with 2+ leaf pairs] --> B[Cut just above a node]
  B --> C[Two axillary shoots grow]
  C --> D[Repeat on each new stem]
  D --> E[Bushy plant + harvested tips]
```

## Chives {#sec-chives}

*(ciboulette)*

- **Light:** morning sun; tolerates the east-facing shade later in the
  day.
- **Water:** moderate — let the top centimetre dry, then water.
- **Care:** see **Trimming** below. Divide clumps in spring if the
  pot is packed.
- **Support:** none. A clump in a 15–20 cm pot is enough.
- **Companions:** basil and parsley (they like similar moisture).

### Trimming chives for harvest {#sec-chives-trim}

Treat it like a haircut, as in
[Les Sourciers — how to prune chives](https://lessourciers.com/fr/blog/2024/10/07/taille-ciboulette/):
cut the whole tuft, do not pluck a few tubes.

1. First cut when the leaves are about **15 cm**.
2. In spring and summer, cut every **two weeks**.
3. Shear **a few centimetres above the soil** with scissors or
   secateurs. Leave that stub so the plant can regrow; cutting flush
   often yellows the new shoots.
4. In autumn, one shorter cut helps it into winter. In a Marseille
   winter you can keep harvesting lightly; if a hard frost is
   forecast, stop cutting and mulch the crown.
5. If the clump is dense and stays wet, divide it: lift a wedge with
   roots and pot it on. Crowded, uncut chives hold moisture and can
   rot.

Use the cut leaves fresh, freeze in portions, or dry. The purple
flowers are edible.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-chives-trim
%%| fig-cap: "Chives: shear the tuft a few centimetres above the crown."
flowchart TD
  A[Leaves ~15 cm] --> B[Shear 2–3 cm above soil]
  B --> C[Regrowth in ~2 weeks]
  C --> B
  B --> D[Divide if the clump is packed]
```

## Thyme {#sec-thyme}

*(thym)*

- **Light:** the most sun-hungry of this list; place at the brightest
  edge of the balcony.
- **Water:** spare. Allow the compost to dry between waterings.
  Overwatering in a saucer is the usual way to lose thyme here.
- **Substrate:** grittier mix (potting compost plus sand or fine
  gravel). No rich nitrogen feed.
- **Support:** none. See **Trimming** below.
- **Companions:** grow **alone**. It wants drier roots than basil,
  parsley, and dill.

### Trimming thyme for harvest {#sec-thyme-trim}

Thyme lignifies: old brown wood will not resprout.

1. Snip **green tips** only, just above a leaf node, as if taking
   cuttings. Never cut back into bare wood.
2. After flowering, a light all-over trim of the green growth keeps
   the mound dense.
3. Do not “mow” the plant to a stump. If it becomes woody and sparse,
   start a new plant from a tip cutting rather than hard-pruning.
4. Harvest little and often through the growing season; a large
   one-off cut in midsummer can kill a pot-grown plant in heat.

## Dill {#sec-dill}

*(aneth)*

- **Light:** morning sun; it bolts (runs to flower) fast in Marseille
  heat, so successive small sowings work better than one large plant.
- **Water:** regular, like parsley; do not let the pot bake.
- **Support:** stems are brittle — a thin cane or a ring of string
  once the plant is above about 30 cm.
- **Care:** see **Trimming** below.
- **Companions:** own pot. Dill can inhibit some neighbours and grows
  tall enough to shade basil.

### Trimming dill for harvest {#sec-dill-trim}

Dill is a short-lived annual. You harvest foliage; you cannot turn
it into a perennial bush like basil.

1. Take **young leaves** by snipping whole side stems, not by
   stripping the main axis bald.
2. For a leaf crop, cut before the flower umbel opens — flavour
   drops and the plant then puts energy into seed.
3. Leave one plant to flower if you want seeds (pickles) or to feed
   hoverflies.
4. In Marseille heat it bolts fast: sow a pinch every two to three
   weeks rather than relying on one plant.
5. When a stem is for the vase or the kitchen, cut it near the base;
   the remaining seedlings in the pot will take over.

## Curly parsley {#sec-parsley}

*(persil frisé)*

- **Light:** morning sun and afternoon shade suit it; it scorches in
  full south or west sun in July.
- **Water:** never let the compost dry out. Deep pot (taproot): 20 cm
  or more.
- **Humidity:** appreciates a light mist in dry wind, like basil.
- **Support:** none. See **Trimming** below.
- **Companions:** basil and chives. Slow to germinate — buy a seedling
  if you want a crop this month.

### Trimming curly parsley for harvest {#sec-parsley-trim}

Parsley grows from a central crown. If you cut that, the plant stops.

1. Always take **outer stems**, cutting them at the base (soil
   level), not halfway up the stalk.
2. Leave the inner, paler shoots — they are next week’s leaves.
3. Harvest regularly; neglected plants send up a flower stalk
   (biennial) and then the leaf quality falls.
4. If a flower stalk appears, cut it out at the base unless you want
   seed. Start a replacement pot: parsley in a container is not
   worth keeping once it has bolted in summer heat.

## Quick reference {#sec-herb-table}

| Herb | Moisture | Harvest cut | Same pot as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basil | High | Above a leaf-pair node | Parsley, chives |
| Chives | Medium | Shear 2–3 cm above soil | Basil, parsley |
| Thyme | Low | Green tips only; never old wood | Alone |
| Dill | Medium–high | Side stems; before the umbel | Alone |
| Curly parsley | High | Outer stems at the crown | Basil, chives |

: Herb care on an east-facing Marseille balcony. {#tbl-herb-care}

```{mermaid}

flowchart LR
  A[Morning sun on balcony] --> B{Compost dry?}
  B -->|Basil / parsley / dill| C[Water that evening]
  B -->|Chives| D[Water if top cm is dry]
  B -->|Thyme| E[Wait — water twice a week]
  C --> F[Trim basil at a node; shear chives; outer parsley stems]
  D --> F
```
